Many apps carry code from advertising and analytics companies. A scan looks inside each app for the ones Exodus Privacy has catalogued. It is done on this phone with a list that is built into the launcher. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Lets the launcher open the notification shade and lock the screen.

Privacy Launcher uses this only to open the notification shade and to lock the screen, because Android gives no other way to do either. It is registered for no accessibility events at all and cannot read the contents of any screen — the system refuses it that capability. Nothing is logged, stored or sent anywhere. The launcher works fully without this; only the swipe-down and double-tap gestures need it.
Swipe down for notifications and double-tap to lock need an accessibility service, because Android offers apps no other way. It reads nothing and stores nothing — tap to read exactly what it can do.
On. Swipe down for notifications, double-tap to lock.
On. Swipe down for notifications. Double-tap to lock needs Android 9 or later, which this phone does not have.
Off. Those two gestures do nothing until you turn it on.

Android does not let an ordinary app open the notification shade or lock the screen. An accessibility service can, so that is what this one is for.

It is set up as narrowly as Android allows:

• It is registered for no accessibility events, so the system never tells it what is on screen.
• It cannot read window content. The system refuses it that capability; it is not a promise we are making.
• It performs exactly two actions: open notifications, and lock the screen.

Nothing is logged, stored or sent anywhere. You can turn it off at any time in Android's accessibility settings, and the launcher keeps working — those two gestures simply stop.

What focus does, and does not do

Focus hides apps. It does not block them.

A set-aside app is still installed and still running whatever it was running. It can still be opened from a notification, from a link in another app, or from a different launcher. Only this launcher's home screen and drawer stop offering it.

The launcher's own screens are never hidden, so you can always get back here and switch focus off.

Nothing runs in the background to make this work. There is no alarm and no background service: the launcher simply looks at the clock when you look at the launcher.
Pick a few apps and set the rest aside, by hand or on a daily schedule.
On. Tap to end it or change what is allowed.
A text-only home screen: app names in large type, no icons. Folders are flattened, dock apps join the list, and there is no reordering — switch this off to rearrange.
Four short pages, then you are done. Nothing here asks for a permission, and you can skip the lot — every one of these choices is in Settings afterwards.
Android asks you to pick which app is the home screen. Until you do, pressing Home still goes to your old launcher.
This is already your home screen.
This opens Android\'s own settings screen. You can also do it later from Settings.
These apply as you tap, so choose by looking rather than by reading.
Your wallpaper\'s own colours are an option too, in Settings under Appearance.
What this app does not do
A promise is only worth what can be checked, so each of these is something you can verify yourself.
It has no internet permission at all. Not unused — absent. It cannot reach the network even if it tried.

It asks for two permissions, Contacts and Modify system settings, and neither does anything until you switch on the feature that needs it. A third in the manifest is generated by a library and is signature-level: it only lets the app talk to itself, and nothing else on the phone can hold it.
Everything it knows stays in its own private storage on this phone. Cloud backup and device transfer are switched off.
No analytics, no crash reporting, no ads, no Google Play Services. Every library it uses is open source.
Write your settings and home layout to a file you choose. No cloud, no account.
The file holds your preferences and home layout. It does not include your usage record or a running focus session.
